seats.name: seat-1
argv:
Read spec.txt (the STAMP language) and program.stamp. Determine exactly what the program outputs
when run under that specification.

Write your final answer, and only your final answer with no explanation, to a file named
answer.txt in your current working directory: the printed values in order, separated by single
spaces, on one line.

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-1 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room agreed 3/3 on the answer, and I wrote it to `answer.txt` and left the room. I traced the program by hand rather than running an interpreter.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

My first trace had the second-to-last value as 101, and seat-3 caught it. Inside `outer`, the call to `inner` can't see `outer`'s local `a`, so it reads the global `a`, which is 0. That gives 0 + 100 = 100, not 101.

seats.text:
The program's output is below. The room concluded 3/3 on that exact text (`prop_5d56f2db`), and I've left the room.

`answer.txt` in the workspace holds the same line:

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`

I got this by hand-tracing `program.stamp` against `spec.txt`; I did not run an interpreter. The other two seats traced it independently and matched.

The only disagreement was the second-to-last value, `CALL outer 1`. Seat-1 first had 101, but `inner` is a separate call, so it can't see `outer`'s local `a`. It reads the global `a`, which is 0, giving 100. Seat-1 corrected it.

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`
